title: Property, Plant & Equipment
description: Account for acquisition costs, depreciation, disposals, exchanges, impairment and presentation of long-lived tangible assets.
html:
Property, Plant & Equipment

Property, plant, and equipment are long-lived tangible assets used in operations. For FAR, you should understand initial cost, depreciation, subsequent expenditures, disposals, exchanges, and impairment.

1. Initial Measurement

PP&E is generally recorded at the cost necessary to acquire the asset and prepare it for its intended use.

  • Purchase price
  • Freight and transportation costs
  • Installation and testing costs
  • Legal fees directly related to acquisition
  • Certain site preparation costs

2. Land

Land is generally not depreciated because it normally has an indefinite useful life.

Costs necessary to prepare land for use are generally included in the cost of land.

Examples can include purchase price, title fees, commissions, and certain clearing or grading costs.

3. Land Improvements

Land improvements with limited useful lives are generally recorded separately from land and depreciated.

Examples

  • Parking lots
  • Fences
  • Lighting systems
  • Private roads

4. Depreciation

Depreciation systematically allocates the depreciable cost of a long-lived asset over its estimated useful life.

Depreciable Base = Cost − Estimated Residual Value

Straight-Line Method

Annual Depreciation = Cost − Residual Value ÷ Useful Life

Example

Equipment cost: $110,000

Residual value: $10,000

Useful life: 5 years

($110,000 − $10,000) ÷ 5 = $20,000 annual depreciation

5. Book Value

Carrying Amount = Asset Cost − Accumulated Depreciation

Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account.

6. Changes in Depreciation Estimates

Changes in useful life or residual value are generally treated as changes in accounting estimates.

Changes in estimates are generally applied prospectively.

7. Subsequent Expenditures

Expenditures after acquisition may be capitalized or expensed depending on their nature.

  • Routine repairs and maintenance are generally expensed.
  • Expenditures that extend useful life, increase capacity, or improve future economic benefits may be capitalized.

8. Disposal of PP&E

When an asset is sold, the company removes the asset's cost and accumulated depreciation and compares the proceeds with the asset's carrying amount.

Gain or Loss = Cash Proceeds − Carrying Amount

Example

Equipment cost: $80,000

Accumulated depreciation: $50,000

Carrying amount: $30,000

Asset sold for: $36,000

$36,000 − $30,000 = $6,000 gain

9. Asset Retirement Obligations

Certain long-lived assets may create a legal obligation to retire, dismantle, remove, or restore property in the future.

When the applicable recognition criteria are met, the company recognizes an asset retirement obligation as a liability and generally capitalizes a corresponding asset retirement cost as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived asset.

  • The capitalized asset retirement cost is generally allocated to expense over the asset's useful life.
  • The ARO liability generally increases over time because of the passage of time.
  • Changes in the estimated timing or amount of the retirement obligation may also require adjustment.

10. Impairment

Long-lived assets held and used must be evaluated for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that their carrying amount may not be recoverable.

For U.S. GAAP long-lived assets held and used, the impairment model generally begins with a recoverability test using undiscounted cash flows.

If the asset is not recoverable, the impairment loss is generally measured as the excess of carrying amount over fair value.

11. CPA Exam Focus

  • Know which acquisition costs are capitalized.
  • Remember that land is generally not depreciated.
  • Calculate depreciation and carrying amount.
  • Treat changes in useful life as changes in estimate.
  • Distinguish capital expenditures from repairs.
  • Calculate gains and losses on disposal.
  • Understand the basic U.S. GAAP impairment model.

quiz.prompt: Equipment cost $90,000 and has accumulated depreciation of $54,000. The equipment is sold for $41,000. What gain or loss should be recognized?
quiz.explanation: The equipment's carrying amount is $90,000 minus $54,000, or $36,000. Because the equipment is sold for $41,000, the company recognizes a $5,000 gain.

objectives: Explain property, plant & equipment and its underlying principles.
